patient.chief_complaint: Six weeks of progressive headaches, word-finding difficulty, and left-sided visual field deficit
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Khalid Al-Rashidi is a 57-year-old right-handed civil engineer who presents to the inpatient neurology service with a six-week history of progressive headaches, word-finding difficulty, and a visual field problem that his wife first noticed while they were driving. He reports that the headaches began insidiously approximately six weeks ago as a dull, pressure-like sensation localized predominantly to the right temporal and parietal region. Initially, he attributed them to work-related stress and inadequate sleep. Over the subsequent two weeks, the headaches became more persistent, occurring daily, and were notably worse upon awakening in the morning. Acetaminophen provided minimal relief. He began avoiding bright light and found himself retreating to quiet, darkened rooms, which he attributed to what he assumed was a migraine variant — he had no prior history of migraine. Approximately four weeks ago, his wife noticed that he was struggling to find words during dinner conversations, occasionally substituting descriptive phrases for objects he should have easily named. He acknowledged this difficulty but minimized it, attributing it to fatigue. Two weeks ago, she observed that he repeatedly failed to notice a car approaching from the left upper side while seated in the passenger seat, and he subsequently stopped driving out of caution. He has experienced three episodes in the past month that he describes as brief 'freezing' spells lasting ten to fifteen seconds, during which he stares blankly and is unresponsive; his wife noticed slight lip-smacking during one of these episodes. He did not seek medical attention immediately after these events, attributing the first to exhaustion and the second to hypoglycemia given his diabetes. At his primary care follow-up one week ago, brief cognitive testing revealed anomic errors, and his physician identified the left visual field deficit on confrontation testing. Emergency brain MRI was ordered, which demonstrated a right temporal lobe mass. He was admitted for urgent neurological evaluation. He denies frank hemiplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, nausea, vomiting, or unintentional weight loss. He has not had fever, chills, or recent infections. He has no known history of malignancy or immunosuppression. He was born and raised in Jordan and emigrated to the United States 22 years ago.

results.title: High-grade gliomas with mesenchymal/sarcomatous differentiation: clinicopathological features and outcomes
results.summary: Gliosarcoma is a rare variant of IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (WHO grade 4) accounting for 2-8% of all glioblastomas. It is characterized by a biphasic histology with alternating glial (GFAP-positive) and sarcomatous (reticulin-rich, vimentin-positive) components. Gliosarcoma has a predilection for the temporal lobe and occurs predominantly in the sixth to seventh decades with a male preponderance. Molecular features mirror IDH-wildtype GBM: TERT promoter mutations, EGFR amplification, and +7/-10 chromosomal changes. MGMT methylation is present in approximately 25% of cases. Median overall survival ranges from 14-18 months with combined modality therapy.

results.title: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System 2021: Key Updates for High-Grade Gliomas
results.summary: The 2021 WHO CNS tumor classification integrates molecular markers with histology. Gliosarcoma is classified as a histological variant of glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4. IDH-wildtype status is defined by absence of IDH1/IDH2 mutations. Molecular criteria for glioblastoma include TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/-10 chromosome changes in the presence of IDH-wildtype astrocytoma of any grade. MGMT promoter methylation remains the strongest predictor of benefit from temozolomide.

results.title: Surgical management and prognostic factors in adult high-grade gliomas: multi-center analysis
results.summary: Maximal safe surgical resection followed by concurrent chemoradiation (temozolomide 75 mg/m2 with 60 Gy in 30 fractions) and adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2, 5 days per 28-day cycle) is the standard of care for gliosarcoma, mirroring the Stupp protocol for GBM. Extent of resection (gross total vs. subtotal) is the strongest surgical prognostic factor (OS 17.2 vs. 11.4 months, p<0.001). Pre-operative functional MRI and DTI tractography are critical for resection planning in tumors adjacent to eloquent cortex or white matter tracts.

output.proposed: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily (seizure prophylaxis) + Dexamethasone 4 mg IV every 6 hours (cerebral edema)
interactions: Levetiracetam + Dexamethasone: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Dexamethasone may reduce levetiracetam plasma levels marginally via CYP induction; clinical significance is low at standard doses. Monitor seizure control.

Dexamethasone + Metformin: Dexamethasone causes dose-dependent hyperglycemia, which may worsen glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes. Close blood glucose monitoring is required; insulin supplementation is likely needed during steroid course.
Dexamethasone + Sitagliptin: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction; however, steroid-induced hyperglycemia may reduce effectiveness of non-insulin agents; insulin initiation is often required.
Levetiracetam + Atorvastatin: No clinically significant interaction.
Aspirin + Levetiracetam: No significant interaction; however, aspirin should be used with caution in the perioperative period given bleeding risk.
contraindications: Do not use enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital) concurrently with temozolomide: these reduce temozolomide efficacy and increase hematologic toxicity; levetiracetam is the preferred AED in this context
Avoid trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PCP prophylaxis in patients with sulfonamide hypersensitivity — this patient has no known drug allergies, so TMP-SMX may be used
warnings: Steroid-induced hyperglycemia: monitor fasting and postprandial blood glucose at minimum four times daily during dexamethasone course; sliding scale insulin and possible insulin initiation required
Levetiracetam behavioral toxicity (irritability, mood changes): monitor for psychiatric side effects, especially in patients with pre-existing behavioral symptoms
Thromboembolic risk: glioma patients are at high risk for VTE; consider pharmacologic prophylaxis with enoxaparin once surgical hemostasis is confirmed
Perioperative aspirin management: consider holding aspirin 7-10 days before craniotomy to reduce intraoperative bleeding risk; resume postoperatively at discretion of neurosurgery team

differential.key_features: Classic GBM is the closest mimic; gliosarcoma is a histological variant distinguishable only by biopsy demonstrating the biphasic glial-sarcomatous pattern with GFAP-positive/reticulin-negative glial component and GFAP-negative/reticulin-positive sarcomatous component

Intratumoral hemorrhage on MRI is more common in metastases (melanoma, RCC, choriocarcinoma, thyroid); however, no known primary malignancy, staging CT negative, and imaging infiltrative margins favor primary brain tumor

PCNSL typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and low perfusion; heterogeneous ring enhancement with internal hemorrhage and elevated rCBV are atypical for lymphoma in this immunocompetent patient

No fever, no leukocytosis, no infectious source; mildly elevated CRP/ESR non-specific; DWI restriction is central (pus) in abscess but is peripheral (rim) in this case; elevated rCBV inconsistent with abscess

Internal hemorrhage, complete ring enhancement, very high rCBV, and age/sex profile are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions typically show incomplete 'open' ring enhancement and low perfusion

key_reasoning_points: Progressive headache worse in the morning, new focal neurological deficits (anomia, left upper quadrantanopia, left pronator drift, Babinski sign), and witnessed staring spells in an adult over age 50 constitute a red-flag syndrome mandating urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

The right temporal location with optic radiation (Meyer's loop) involvement explains the left upper homonymous quadrantanopia — a localizing sign to the right temporal lobe that should direct the diagnostic workup

Internal hemorrhagic foci on MRI expand the imaging differential to include hemorrhagic metastasis, but the infiltrative margins, absence of a known primary, negative staging CT, and markedly elevated peritumoral rCBV on perfusion MRI favor a primary glioma

Gliosarcoma is a histological variant of IDH-wildtype GBM (WHO grade 4) defined by a biphasic glial-sarcomatous pattern; it cannot be distinguished from classic GBM on imaging alone — the sarcomatous component may contribute to hemorrhagic tendency and MRI heterogeneity

Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV >4) and MR spectroscopy (Cho/NAA ratio 10.3, elevated peritumoral choline) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and tumor infiltration beyond the enhancing margin, supporting tissue targeting for biopsy and ruling out abscess

The right temporal-parietal location adjacent to the arcuate fasciculus and Meyer's loop mandates pre-operative functional MRI with DTI tractography to guide maximal safe resection and minimize language/visual morbidity

Mass effect (4 mm midline shift, sylvian fissure effacement) makes lumbar puncture contraindicated despite the mildly elevated inflammatory markers — LP herniation risk takes precedence over any diagnostic yield

Mild thrombocytopenia (118 x10^9/L), elevated ESR/CRP, and hyperglycemia in a diabetic patient should not redirect the workup toward hematologic malignancy or infection: the platelet count is above the surgical threshold, inflammatory markers are non-specifically elevated by the tumor, and hyperglycemia reflects poor diabetes control not immunosuppression — all are red herrings in the context of a clearly malignant temporal lobe mass

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mildly elevated inflammatory markers are non-specifically elevated in patients with intracranial neoplasia; the absence of fever, leukocytosis, and an infectious source, combined with the DWI pattern (peripheral rather than central restriction), markedly elevated rCBV, and elevated peritumoral choline all argue against abscess and favor high-grade glioma

metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from PMC7170742 (PMID 32341747): 60-year-old male with left parieto-occipital gliosarcoma, biphasic histology (GFAP-positive glial + reticulin/vimentin-positive sarcomatous component), hemorrhagic foci, peripheral rim enhancement. Demographics, location (right temporal), and red-herring constellation authored authentically distinct from the seed case per NeuroBench policy.
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: The internal hemorrhagic foci and imaging heterogeneity introduce a hemorrhagic metastasis as a serious alternative differential requiring active exclusion with staging CT and advanced MRI. Three embedded red herrings (mild thrombocytopenia, elevated inflammatory markers, diabetic immunosuppression) create plausible but spurious pressure toward hematologic or infectious diagnoses. Correct identification of gliosarcoma requires integration of advanced MRI (perfusion + spectroscopy + functional/DTI) with histopathology showing the defining biphasic pattern.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools, 3 recommended tools, 3 embedded red herrings; requires synthesis of MRI + advanced imaging (perfusion, spectroscopy, functional/DTI) + tissue diagnosis; gliosarcoma variant not distinguishable from classic GBM on imaging alone; hemorrhagic appearance expands imaging differential
